title: ANALYSIS | Democrats' dilemma: Investigate Trump or work with him? | CBC News

Investigate Trump or work with him? Democrats debate best path forward

What Dems do with their big majorities in Congress will shape U.S. politics over next two years

Still giddy from their sweeping midterm victory over U.S. President Donald Trump's Republican Party, the Democrats now face a dilemma over what to do next.

Some Democratic factions are urging the party to use its new majorities in the House and Senate to investigate Trump, his family and his allies over allegations of corruption.

Others insist the Democrats must avoid being distracted by trying to score political points against the president and instead stay laser-focused on what voters signalled as their biggest concern: the cost of living.

The path Democrats choose could shape much of U.S. politics over the next two years and influence what happens in the post-Trump presidential election of 2028.

The choices the party faces over its future direction were on full display in Denver, Colo., where a new but well-funded political organization that aims to steer Democrats toward the centre sponsored a conference entitled What's Next.

A long list of Democratic rising stars and power brokers took turns delivering their visions for the party, including the candidate who pulled off arguably the most monumental red-to-blue flip of election night, senator-elect James Talarico of Texas.

James Talarico, senator-elect of Texas, speaks during a conference about the future of the Democratic Party on Thursday in Denver, Colo. (David Zalubowski/The Associated Press)

"We must deliver immediate, bold relief during this affordability crisis. We must unrig this economic system that only benefits the top one per cent," Talarico told the crowd.

He went on to lay out another 10 must-dos, including universal healthcare, overhauling the immigration system and cutting red tape to build millions of new homes, each greeted by raucous applause.

'Work with President Trump'

Talarico then offered a "we must" that stunned the crowd into near silence.

"The American people cannot wait two years for change. So we must work with President Trump," he said.

"We should make the final two years of his presidency the most productive of any presidency in American history, because this moment is so much bigger and so much more important than the red team or the blue team."

Talarico's proposal acknowledges a fundamental reality the Democrats will face when they take control of Congress in January: Trump will still be president, with veto power and executive authority, giving him plenty of scope to thwart the party's agenda.

Yet there's plenty of skepticism that Trump will want to co-operate in any way, prompting some Democrats to argue for a more aggressive approach with the White House aimed at holding the administration accountable.

Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, is vowing "to take on corruption wherever we find it."

He's one of several Democrats with key roles in powerful congressional committees already signalling they intend to investigate a range of the Trump administration's dealings and actions. Among their targets:

  • donations to Trump's pet construction projects, such as the White House ballroom
  • the administration's $1.6-billion US investment in a mining company
  • the Department of Homeland Security's $496-million purchase of a shuttered prison
  • the CIA's expanded use of covert action over the past two years.

Garcia argues it's not a binary choice for Democrats between investigating corruption and reducing the cost of living.

"As families struggle with rising costs, the Trumps are cashing in on the presidency and stealing from the American taxpayer. Taking on their corruption is about making life more affordable," Garcia posted on X.

Robert Garcia, a Democrat from California, is the party's leading member of the House Oversight Committee. He's pictured on the steps of the Capitol in Washington, D.C. on Nov. 10. (J. Scott Applewhite/The Associated Press)

How Democrats navigate this terrain over the next two years matters deeply because it will play into voters' perceptions of the party and its presidential candidate heading into the 2028 election.

They're getting no shortage of advice about how best to approach it. Two pieces published within days of each other in The Atlantic last week illustrate the ends of the spectrum.

'Investigate Trump like a mob boss'

"Democrats should cut a deal with Trump" says the headline of the first, by Villanova University law professor Chaim Saiman. "Investigate Trump like a mob boss" says the headline of the second, by former federal prosecutor Randall Eliason.

The Democrat behind the most shocking win of the midterms, senator-elect Scott Colom of Mississippi, rejects the notion that the party faces an either-or scenario.

"Did Mississippians elect you to work with the president or stand up to him?" CNN's Dana Bash asked Colom on the weekend.

Colom responded by saying voters elected him to ensure Trump follows through on his commitments.

Mississippi Democrat Scott Colom defeated Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith in the midterm election for U.S. Senate. He is seen here speaking to reporters Jackson, Mississippi on Nov. 4. (Lauren Witte/USA Today Network/Reuters)

Trump "promised lower grocery prices on day one. Well, I want to work with him to actually accomplish that," Colom said. "He promised no more endless wars. Well, I want to work with him to accomplish that."

One thing Democrats won't control is how Trump reacts to their tactics.

If Congress puts a bill on his desk with populist measures to rein in the costs of things like health care and housing, will Trump welcome it or veto it?

If the Democrats' investigations start probing Trump or his family a little too closely for the president's comfort, will he go into full-on flamethrower mode, blocking everything that comes from Congress and ordering the Department of Justice to pursue his political enemies?

Democratic leaders are aware that an attempt to impeach Trump would almost certainly fall short of the two-thirds majority needed in the Senate for a conviction.

They're also conscious of the risk that investigations that smack of political grandstanding and appear out of step with Americans' priorities could ultimately backfire with voters.

"The Democratic Party is still very much on probation in vast swaths of this country," Colorado Congressman Jason Crow told National Public Radio at the Denver conference. "It's going to take us more than one [election] cycle to re-earn that trust. So we actually have to deliver for folks now."
